theory.title: TCP: The Three-Way Handshake
theory.recap: You've routed by destination IP, passed firewalls by port number, and even chosen between healthy backends. But none of that has involved talking to the server. TCP is the moment the packet stops being addressed-and-forwarded and starts being part of a real conversation - one that has to begin with a formal handshake.
theory.plainObjective: Route to the firewall, pass on port 80, then complete the three-step handshake in order: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
theory.summary: This three-message exchange happens in the background every time you open a website, send an email, or load any page over TCP - which is almost everything on the internet.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why does TCP exist?
bodyParagraphs.text: IP delivers packets but makes no guarantees - they can be lost, reordered, or duplicated. TCP adds reliability on top. Before any data flows, both sides complete the three-way handshake.

bodyParagraphs.heading: The three steps
bodyParagraphs.text:
• Step 1: client sends SYN (synchronise)
  • Step 2: server replies SYN-ACK (synchronise + acknowledge)
  • Step 3: client sends ACK (acknowledge)
Only then is the connection ESTABLISHED and data can flow.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why can't you skip steps?
bodyParagraphs.text: Each step confirms both sides can send and receive. Sending ACK before receiving SYN-ACK would mean acknowledging something you never saw. TCP rejects out-of-order steps.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Handshake sits on routing
bodyParagraphs.text: TCP runs on top of IP and ports. Routing and firewall rules always apply first. The handshake is a layer above.

termIntroductions.headline: TCP
termIntroductions.body: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a transport protocol that sits above IP. It provides ordered, reliable delivery by establishing a connection before sending data. Most web traffic uses TCP.

termIntroductions.headline: SYN - Synchronise
termIntroductions.body: SYN is the first message in a TCP handshake. The client sends it to say: I want to open a connection. Without SYN, the server has no context for any data that follows.

termIntroductions.headline: SYN-ACK
termIntroductions.body: SYN-ACK is the server's reply. It acknowledges your SYN and sends back its own. This proves the server received your request and is ready to communicate. Now you know the server is alive and listening.

termIntroductions.headline: ESTABLISHED
termIntroductions.body: After you send ACK, the connection state becomes ESTABLISHED. Both sides have confirmed they can send and receive. Only now will the server accept data. This three-message exchange happens in milliseconds on every TCP connection you make.
